title: GitHub Copilot — The First Taste of AI Coding

panels.text: On June 29, 2021, GitHub announced Copilot as a technical preview. Built on OpenAI Codex, a 12-billion-parameter language model fine-tuned on billions of lines of public code, Copilot predicted not just the next word — but entire functions.

panels.prompt: A tech CEO presenting on a large stage, illuminated by a spotlight, behind him a massive screen showing the GitHub Copilot logo and 'June 2021' text, audience in silhouette, atmosphere of a major product launch, excitement and anticipation in the air. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, violet and blue accent lighting

A large glowing digital counter display ticking upward, showing the number '1,000,000' with the label 'Paying Subscribers' below it and 'Feb 2023' above, bright violet neon glow, confetti and celebration particles, sense of massive adoption and milestone, dark background. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, violet (#9F7AEA) accent

panels.text: Copilot became generally available on June 21, 2022, at $10/month. By February 2023: over one million paying subscribers. An internal study claimed developers completed tasks 55% faster. Critics noted the study used a simple task — but nobody disputed the feeling. Developers called it a “before and after” moment.

panels.prompt: A dramatic split composition. Left side: a developer grinning with delight, a glowing code suggestion floating before them, warm golden light, positive energy. Right side: another developer frowning at their screen where a code suggestion shows a familiar GPL license header appearing in the inline suggestion text, red warning glow, concern and suspicion. A jagged dividing line down the center separates the two reactions. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, golden vs red contrast

panels.text: Copilot had been trained on public code, including GPL-licensed code. Lawyer Matthew Butterick filed a class-action lawsuit in November 2022, calling it “software piracy at an unprecedented scale.” The fundamental question: is an AI learning patterns from code the same as copying that code? The legal system is still wrestling with the answer.

panels.text: “If you read a thousand cookbooks and then write your own recipe, is that copying? What if your recipe happens to match someone else’s word for word? At what point does ‘learning from’ become ‘copying’?”
Copilot could finish your sentences. But what if you didn't want to write code at all? What if you just wanted to describe what you needed — in plain English — and have AI write the whole thing?
